sources.title: Navigation Safety Regulations, 2020 (SOR/2020-216), Part 2 Marine Radiocommunications, Schedule 4
sources.publisher: Department of Justice Canada
sources.edition: Consolidation in the XML clone, amendments to 2023-12-20; accessed 2026-10-10
sources.notes: Justice Canada laws-lois XML clone (updated 2026-09-28), read in full as text. Supports: Part 2 definitions (continuous watch, DSC, EPIRB 406 MHz, NAVTEX 518 kHz, PLB, radio operator, SART, sea areas A1 to A4, traffic zone); ss. 204 (VHF-DSC carriage), 206, 209 (EPIRB), 210, 212 (documents), 214 (TP 9878 card, clock), 215, 217, 228 (beacon registry), 230 to 231, 236 to 239 (checks and tests), 240 (radio inspection certificate), 243 to 247 (distress per ITU articles 32 to 34, cancel false alerts, power, time, radio record), 248, 250, 251, 252 (listening watch), 253 (navigation safety calls), Schedule 4 (channels).

sources.title: Marine Personnel Regulations (SOR/2007-115): ss. 131, 216, 254, 266, 267
sources.publisher: Department of Justice Canada
sources.edition: Consolidation in the XML clone; accessed 2026-10-10
sources.notes: Justice Canada laws-lois XML clone (updated 2026-09-28), read in full as text. Supports: s. 131 table (Master, Limited under 60 GT: appropriate radio operator certificate if the vessel has a VHF radiotelephone installation); s. 216(2) (person in charge of the deck watch holds an appropriate radio certificate if VHF is fitted); s. 254 (listening watch at anchor or moored if the vessel may be a hazard); s. 266 (who may be in charge of the radio watch: ROC with Maritime Qualification, General Operator or ROC-MC; ROC-MC needed on a DSC voyage other than sheltered waters, with a Near Coastal Class 2 exception); s. 267 (principal communicator, 300 GT or more).

sources.title: Canada Shipping Act, 2001 (S.C. 2001, c. 26): ss. 112 and 131
sources.publisher: Department of Justice Canada
sources.edition: Consolidation in the XML clone; accessed 2026-10-10
sources.notes: Justice Canada laws-lois XML clone (updated 2026-09-28), read in full as text. Supports: s. 112 (master who meets dangerous ice, a derelict or other direct danger, a tropical storm, winds of force 10 or more on the Beaufort scale for which no storm warning was received, or subfreezing air with gale-force winds and severe icing must give notice to vessels nearby and the prescribed authorities ashore); s. 131 (duty to proceed with all speed to assist on receiving a distress signal and to inform the persons in distress or sender if possible; release and requisition rules; log book entry if not proceeding).

sources.title: Small Vessel Regulations (SOR/2010-91): ss. 404, 501, 717(4)
sources.publisher: Department of Justice Canada
sources.edition: Consolidation in the XML clone (header 2026-01-20); accessed 2026-10-10
sources.notes: Justice Canada laws-lois XML clone (updated 2026-09-28), read in full as text. Supports: s. 404 (a passenger-carrying vessel of not more than 15 GT with not more than 12 passengers must be designed and equipped to operate safely in its area of operation; no person shall operate it under circumstances that exceed its design limitations, if any); s. 501 (same two duties for a workboat); s. 717(4) (builder or importer gives the end user a document setting out the design limitations, if any, including capacity, power and environmental limitations). Does not define the limits for any particular vessel.

sources.title: Radio Aids to Marine Navigation (RAMN) 2026, general part (VHF, DSC, distress, urgency and safety procedures, sea areas)
sources.publisher: Canadian Coast Guard
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: Ch 16 (156.800 MHz) and 2182 kHz only for distress, urgency, safety and calling; initial calls on Ch 16 because MCTS centres do not monitor working channels; DSC on Ch 70 (156.525 MHz); MAYDAY, PAN PAN and SECURITE meanings and call and message formats; priority of distress; mayday relay conditions; SEELONCE FEENEE and OUT; 3 minute listening after PAN PAN; no acknowledgement of an all-stations DSC safety announcement; DSC distress alert by holding the red button 5 seconds then voice on Ch 16; alerts and relays only with the master's permission; no DSC relay after receiving a VHF or MF DSC distress alert; MMSI must be programmed; steps to cancel a false alert; sea areas with A1 about 40 nm and A2 about 150 nm; West Coast A1 about 40 nm offshore; time in four figures, UTC preferred; EPIRB test every 6 months. The last 12,694 characters of the page were not read. Ch 13 does not appear in the part read.

sources.title: Radio Aids to Marine Navigation 2024, Part 2: Facilities Information (Victoria and Prince Rupert MCTS)
sources.publisher: Canadian Coast Guard
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: Victoria MCTS (call sign VAK, MMSI 003160011) and Prince Rupert MCTS (call sign VAJ, MMSI 003160013), both 24 hours and English only; BC remote sites mostly on Ch 11, 12, 16, 70, 83A; Continuous Marine Broadcast on Ch 21B plus weather channels WX1 to WX3; Victoria weather and CMB schedule; NAVTEX 518 kHz from Digby Island and Amphitrite Point. Does not describe calling procedure or WX frequencies.

sources.title: Radio Aids to Marine Navigation 2024, Part 5: Meteorological information, Pacific coast section 5.14
sources.publisher: Canadian Coast Guard / Environment and Climate Change Canada
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: Pacific Storm Prediction Centre (Vancouver) issues marine forecast and technical synopsis four times a day at 04:00, 10:30, 16:00 and 21:30 (PDT or PST); wave height forecast and extended forecast at 04:00 and 16:00; marine weather statement as needed; forecasts valid to midnight of the following day; NAVTEX Prince Rupert via Amphitrite Point and Digby Island; warning classes 20 to 33, 34 to 47, 48 to 63 and 64 or more knots; strong wind warnings issued from March 20 to Remembrance Day for six named inner waters; Pacific marine forecast area names (Explorer, Bowie, Dixon Entrance, West Coast Haida Gwaii, Queen Charlotte Sound, Hecate Strait, Douglas Channel, West Coast Vancouver Island North and South, Juan de Fuca Strait, Haro Strait, Howe Sound, Strait of Georgia, Johnstone Strait, Queen Charlotte Strait, Central Coast); lists Weatheradio transmitters and a Hello Weather phone service. The page itself is inconsistent about the number of Weatheradio stations.

sources.title: RIC-25: Syllabus for the Restricted Operator's Certificate, Maritime Commercial (ROC-MC)
sources.publisher: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: ROC-MC is for mariners serving on compulsorily fitted commercial ships in Sea Area A1 with VHF; minimum age 18; valid for life; pass mark 70 percent; syllabus areas (VHF/DSC, MMSI, sea areas, watchkeeping on Ch 70 and Ch 16, DSC call categories distress, urgency, safety, ship's business and routine, record keeping, cancelling false alerts, SART and EPIRB, NAVTEX, distress relay).

sources.title: Professional Radio Operator Certificate Services: frequently asked questions
sources.publisher: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: anyone operating a marine radio in Canada needs at least an ROC-M (Restricted Operator Certificate, Maritime); the ROC-MC meets that requirement; the ROC-M is issued by Canadian Power and Sail Squadrons under delegated authority. The page was last modified 2017-01-17 and does not give pass marks or validity for the ROC-M.

sources.title: Boat-Ed Canada study guide: VHF marine radio channels
sources.publisher: Boat-Ed (commercial boating-course provider)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports (provider-level evidence only): Ch 16 distress and hailing, monitored by all MCTS centres; Ch 70 is the DSC alert channel and each radio needs a nine-digit MMSI, assigned free; Ch 13 intership navigational traffic, bridge-to-bridge; Ch 21B and 83B carry English Continuous Marine Broadcast. The channel list quoted is for Central and Arctic MCTS, so BC-specific channel use is not confirmed.

sources.title: Canadian marine warning program, chapter 1 (wind warnings)
sources.publisher: Environment and Climate Change Canada
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: four wind warning categories (strong wind 20 to 33 knots, gale 34 to 47, storm 48 to 63, hurricane force 64 or greater), thresholds exclude gusts; hurricane force warning does not mean a hurricane; warnings use the keyword 'in effect'; strong wind warnings mainly in the recreational boating season for coastal and inland waters; Pacific program March 20 to November 11 for Juan de Fuca Strait, Haro Strait, Howe Sound, Strait of Georgia, Johnstone Strait and Queen Charlotte Strait. Page issued 2013-01-25 and last modified 2014-07-18, so dates may be out of date. Does not cover squall or freezing spray warnings.

sources.title: Marine weather products and services: Pacific coast
sources.publisher: Environment and Climate Change Canada
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: product list (regular forecast days 1 to 2, extended days 3 to 5, technical marine synopsis, marine weather statement, wave height forecast, NAVTEX forecast); issue times 4:00, 10:30, 16:00, 21:30 (regular and synopsis) and 4:00 and 16:00 (extended and wave); wind in knots, average over open water, direction the wind blows from, relative to true north; weather and visibility described near or below 1 nautical mile; air temperature only at or below 0 C; significant wave height is the average of the highest one-third of waves and maximum waves may be up to twice it; warning classes; freezing spray warning at ice build-up of 0.7 cm per hour or more; forecast consultation phone numbers. The page says Weatheradio and Hello Weather are no longer in service, while RAMN 2024 still lists them; the page's modified date is 2017-06-30, so treat it as old.

sources.title: Beaufort wind scale table
sources.publisher: Environment and Climate Change Canada
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: force 0 to 12 names, knot and km/h ranges (0 calm under 1; 1 light air 1 to 3; 2 light breeze 4 to 6; 3 gentle breeze 7 to 10; 4 moderate breeze 11 to 16; 5 fresh breeze 17 to 21; 6 strong breeze 22 to 27; 7 near gale 28 to 33; 8 gale 34 to 40; 9 strong gale 41 to 47; 10 storm 48 to 55; 11 violent storm 56 to 63; 12 hurricane 64 to 71) and sea and land effects. The summariser reported no wave-height column.

sources.title: Guide to Environment Canada marine weather forecasts (reading marine forecasts)
sources.publisher: Environment and Climate Change Canada
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: order of items in a regular forecast (title block, fog statement, area name, warnings and watches, then wind, weather and visibility, freezing spray, air temperature); extended forecast is wind only; wave bulletin is separate; wind is mean at 10 m, direction one of eight points, gusts stated when the mean is expected to rise by 10 knots or more for short periods; synoptic warnings use mean wind only; fog implies visibility under 1 mile; weather stated only if visibility 1 nautical mile or less; freezing spray moderate 0.7 to 2 cm/h, severe above 2 cm/h; air temperature stated only at or below zero; waves in metres and 'seas' for ocean waters; time-of-day definitions (today, tonight, morning 6:00 to 11:59, afternoon noon to 5:59, evening 6:00 to 11:59 p.m., overnight midnight to 5:59); unchanged elements are not repeated; map colours red warning, yellow watch, grey advisory; ice warnings come from the Canadian Ice Service. Some content is general to all regions, not only the Pacific.

sources.title: Pacific - South Coast: regional summary (marine weather)
sources.publisher: Environment and Climate Change Canada
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports only: the Pacific - South Coast area lists 20 marine areas including split areas (for example Strait of Georgia north and south of Nanaimo, Juan de Fuca Strait west entrance, central strait and east entrance, Queen Charlotte Sound eastern and western halves). The page timestamp was 25 June 2026 and it showed a data error for forecasts.

sources.title: Environment Canada Pacific marine forecast bulletin FQCN13 CWVR (text product)
sources.publisher: Environment and Climate Change Canada (via NOAA tgftp mirror)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports only the layout of the text bulletin: header code FQCN13 CWVR with day and UTC time, issuance statement, fixed fog definition, area name in capitals, then warning line, then wind lines by time period in knots, REMAINDER UNCHANGED and END markers. Wording example seen: wind northwest 25 to 35 knots becoming northwest 20 to 30 late this morning. The bulletin date was not shown (day 9 of an unknown month).

sources.title: ATSC 113 8a: Wave formation
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: wave size depends on wind velocity, fetch and duration acting together; a travelling storm effectively lengthens fetch.

sources.title: ATSC 113 8d: Swell
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: swell is waves made by distant storms that travel long distances; longer period means more energy (a 6 ft swell at 15 s can break larger than at 7 s); local wind on swell makes a confused sea; direction is where the swell comes from; Canada forecasts in metres; running parallel to swell causes violent rolling.

sources.title: ATSC 113 8e: Beaufort scale
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: Beaufort force, knots and approximate wave heights in feet for forces 4 to 12 (4: 1 to 4 ft; 5: 4 to 8; 6: 8 to 13; 7: 13 to 19; 8: 18 to 25; 9: 23 to 32; 10: 29 to 41; 11: 37 to 52; 12: over 45); sea descriptions.

sources.title: ATSC 113 9b: Jet streams and mid-latitude cyclones
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: lows form east of a trough and highs east of a ridge; Northern Hemisphere winds turn counterclockwise around lows (air converges and rises) and clockwise around highs (air sinks and diverges); lows bring cloud, rain, fronts and strong wind, highs light wind and clear skies; best sailing is often between a low and a high.

sources.title: ATSC 113 9f: Extratropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, squall lines, waterspouts
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: BC winter lows come every 1 to 4 days, many form over the Kuroshio and occlude before reaching the Gulf of Alaska and BC; atmospheric rivers bring heavy rain ahead of an occluding low; squall lines form along or ahead of a cold front, typically 10 to 15 km wide; waterspouts are not columns of water; downbursts.

sources.title: ATSC 113 9g: Highs, lows and fronts from the water
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: high centre gives light unreliable wind, low centre strong wind and high waves; larger pressure gradient means stronger winds; wind against waves and current gives choppy confused seas.

sources.title: ATSC 113 10a: Local winds (sea breeze, land breeze, katabatic, barrier jet)
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: sea breeze needs a land-sea temperature difference of 5 C or more, usually under high pressure with weak synoptic wind, strongest midday to mid-afternoon, typical coast speed about 22 km/h; land breeze at night; katabatic winds flow down valleys on clear nights and can gush out over water; BC barrier jet along the coast ahead of a cold front. Does not cover gap winds or thermal lows.

sources.title: ATSC 113 10b: Inflows and outflows in coastal inlets
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: inflow is air from the water into inlets and valleys (summer, usually not strong), outflow is air out of the mountains toward the water; summer outflows at night can be strong and hazardous; winter outflows from cold interior air are very strong; Howe Sound (Squamish wind) outflow overnight and early morning switching to afternoon inflow; Qualicum wind 16 to 20 knots versus 2 to 8 knots elsewhere in the Strait of Georgia; outflows can create rough water at inlet mouths while nearby water is calm; warnings state whether wind is inflow or outflow.

sources.title: ATSC 113 10d: Local tides and currents
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: wind with current gives calmer seas and wind against current rougher seas; a turning tide can build waves 'out of nowhere' with no change in wind; passes can be navigable at slack but not at peak flow; Sechelt (Skookumchuk) Rapids up to 17.6 knots; slack water, two high and two low slacks a day, peak currents midway between high and low tide.

sources.title: ATSC 113 10e: Coastal upwelling and fog
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: advection (sea) fog is warm humid air over cooler water, the main sea fog and a navigation hazard, enhanced by upwelling, any time of year; radiation fog forms over land at night; frontal fog; sea smoke is not a navigation hazard; August known as 'Fogust' where mornings are foggy; fog forms as air cools past its dew point; wind and sun dissipate fog; sound signals and radar advice. Gives no visibility distances.

sources.title: ATSC 113 11a: Marine weather forecasts
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: ECCC marine forecast first stop; warnings appear first; detailed 48 hours then outlook; CMB loops through all areas and resets to the newest forecast at 04:00, 10:30, 16:00 and 21:30; CMB also carries station identity, distress and urgency information, ice reports, notices to shipping and weekly mean water levels. The page is inconsistent about the length of the extended forecast.

sources.title: ATSC 113 11b: Weather warnings
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: synoptic warning thresholds; localized warnings (tornado, squall, waterspout, special marine) and watches; squall warning is for gusts above 34 knots tied to a line of storm clouds; freezing spray happens when spray freezes on contact, salt water needs air colder than about minus 2 C, and ice raises the centre of gravity; wind warnings say whether outflow or inflow.

sources.title: ATSC 113 11c: Reading weather maps and forecasting
sources.publisher: UBC Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, ATSC 113 Weather for Sailing, Flying and Snow Sports (course web page)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: lows are bad weather and highs good; average pressure about 101.3 kPa, highs near 103 and lows near 100; 10 mb = 10 hPa = 1 kPa; front symbols and typical weather; isobars close together mean strong wind; winds blow nearly parallel to isobars crossing slightly toward low pressure with low on the left in the Northern Hemisphere; falling barometer means an approaching low or front, rising means an approaching high; analysis versus forecast maps; the author's opinion not to trust a winter Pacific forecast beyond 1 to 2 days.

sources.title: Buys Ballot's Law
sources.publisher: SKYbrary Aviation Safety
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: Northern Hemisphere, stand with your back to the wind and low pressure is on your left and high on your right; stated by C. H. D. Buys Ballot in 1857; only an approximation near the surface because friction turns the wind toward low pressure; does not work near the equator.

sources.title: Fronts (Weather Observation and Analysis course notes, Nielsen-Gammon)
sources.publisher: US National Weather Service, Houston/Galveston training page
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: warm front brings warmer air and rain or snow usually falls ahead of it on the cold side; cold front brings colder air and its cloud and precipitation can be ahead, behind or absent; stationary fronts move very little; occluded front forms near a surface low where the air ahead of a warm front meets the air behind a cold front and its weather resembles a warm front; squall lines can move faster than the front. The source does not use veer or back.

sources.title: Cold front (Wikipedia)
sources.publisher: Wikimedia Foundation
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports (evidence only, not authoritative): in the Northern Hemisphere wind veers from southwest to northwest through a cold front; pressure falls as it approaches then rises sharply; temperature drops; cold fronts move faster than warm fronts. Does not describe warm front wind changes.

sources.title: Wind against current (glossary)
sources.publisher: PredictWind
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: moving water shortens and steepens wind-driven waves, giving confused choppy seas that feel worse than the wind alone suggests; problem spots include headlands, bars, harbour entrances and narrow channels; consider delaying or timing for slack water. Gives no numbers.

sources.title: Sailing Directions PAC 200, General Information, Pacific Coast (opening chapters only)
sources.publisher: Canadian Hydrographic Service
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports only a few remarks in the part the summariser could see (up to Chapter 1): frequent weather changes in Juan de Fuca Strait; strong gales may be frequently encountered in Queen Charlotte Sound and Hecate Strait; heavy swell and dense fog frequent in Fitz Hugh Sound; Dixon Entrance tidal streams treacherous in poor visibility. The meteorology chapter (Chapter 5) and the fog and wind tables were not seen.

sources.title: Search and rescue transponder (Wikipedia)
sources.publisher: Wikimedia Foundation
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports (evidence only): radar SART responds only to 9 GHz X-band radar, an X-band radar within about 8 nautical miles can trigger it, shows 12 dots about 0.64 nm apart that become arcs then circles within about 1 nm; AIS-SART is a GPS-based alternative.

sources.title: EPIRB and SART differences
sources.publisher: Jotron (equipment manufacturer)
sources.notes: Read via an automated summariser (WebFetch), not as full page text. Supports: EPIRB sends a 406 MHz distress signal to Cospas-Sarsat satellites and a 121.5 MHz homing signal, global range, must be registered; SART (radar 9 GHz or AIS) helps rescuers pinpoint survivors, line-of-sight about 8 to 10 nm; EPIRB is a primary alert device and SART a secondary (locating) device.
